slides.headline: How to use *Claude Design* to make designs by chatting

slides.heading: 1. Give it your *brand* first

Then describe the goal, the layout and who it is for.

paragraphs.text: How to use Claude Design, in short: ask Claude for a design, give it your brand and some context, then fix the result on the canvas and export it. Claude Design is a tool from Anthropic Labs that turns a conversation into visual work: app and website mockups, interactive prototypes, slide decks and one-pagers. The work appears on a canvas beside the chat, where you keep editing it.

Anthropic launched Claude Design on April 17, 2026 as a research preview for Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise subscribers. According to the Claude Help Center, it is now available on Free, Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans and is turned on by default.

The point is speed to a first draft. If you are a founder, a product manager or anyone who has to show an idea before a designer has time for it, Claude Design gets you something clickable in minutes. It does not replace a good designer for polished, final work.
Where to open Claude Design

There are four ways in, per the Help Center. In a normal conversation, ask for a design or choose Output, then Design. In the Artifacts tab, pick a Design template. In Claude Code, ask Claude or type /design. On the iOS and Android apps you can create, view and edit designs, but sharing settings have to be changed on the web or the desktop app.
The older standalone version at claude.ai/design closes on December 14, 2026. The Help Center tells users to move their projects and design systems before then.
If you used Claude Design at claude.ai/design earlier this year, move your projects now instead of in December, so you have time to check nothing went missing.
How to use Claude Design, step by step

paragraphs.title: 1. Start a design
paragraphs.text: Open a chat and ask for a design, or go to the Artifacts tab and choose a Design template. Say what you want to make: a landing page, an app screen, a pitch deck, a one-pager.

paragraphs.title: 2. Add a design system
paragraphs.text: A design system holds your colors, typography and components, so every project looks like your brand. You can import one from a GitHub repository, design files, uploads or a local codebase with /design-sync. Projects pick up your organization's design system automatically.

paragraphs.title: 3. Give it context
paragraphs.text: Attach screenshots and other assets, or link a codebase. The more Claude can see of what already exists, the less it guesses.

paragraphs.title: 4. Describe the goal
paragraphs.text: Say what the design is for, the layout you have in mind, the content it must show and who will use it. Mention the target device (phone, laptop, projector) at the start.

paragraphs.title: 5. Review and refine
paragraphs.text: Look at the canvas, then pick the right tool for the change. Use chat for big structural changes or to ask why something was done. Use inline comments for one component. Edit the canvas directly to drag, resize or align things.

paragraphs.title: 6. Export or share
paragraphs.text: Export as a .zip, a PDF, a PowerPoint file, Google Slides or standalone HTML, send it to other tools, or hand it off to Claude Code. Designs are private by default; you can share them with view, comment or edit access.
Anthropic says the handoff to Claude Code packages the finished design into a bundle that Claude Code can build from with a single instruction. Designs can also be exported to Canva.
Prompts that get better designs

Anthropic's own tips are short: import a complete design system, start simple and add detail later, give specific feedback that names the component, mention the target device early, ask for two or three variations, and ask Claude to review accessibility and visual hierarchy.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 1: A first draft with options
paragraphs.text: Design a landing page for [product] aimed at [audience]. Mobile first. Use my design system. Sections: hero with one clear headline, three benefits, pricing, a short FAQ. Give me 3 variations with different layouts.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 2: Feedback that names the part
paragraphs.text: In variation 2, make the pricing cards stack vertically on mobile, move the FAQ above the footer and make the main button in the hero larger. Keep everything else the same.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 3: A slide deck from your numbers
paragraphs.text: Make an 8 slide deck for [meeting] from the attached file. One idea per slide, a chart where the numbers matter, presenter notes on every slide. Use my design system.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 4: A check before you share
paragraphs.text: Review this design for accessibility and visual hierarchy. List every problem you find, from most to least important, then fix the top three.

Check every number Claude puts on a slide against your source. In a hands-on test, TechFinitive found wrong figures and a cropped screenshot in a deck Claude Design made, plus typography problems after export to PowerPoint.
Usage limits and what it is bad at

Claude Design draws on the same usage limits as the rest of Claude, including Claude Code, according to the Help Center. Large codebases and many rounds of changes use more. When you hit the limit, Claude Design stops until the limit resets, unless usage credits are turned on.

Reviewers found the limits to be the main constraint. Writing for Zapier in May 2026, Miguel Rebelo said a Pro plan's weekly allowance could run out in under an hour of work, and that without a custom design system the output tends toward a recognizable look with heavy serif fonts, cards and accent bars.

Anthropic lists its own known limitations: inline comments can sometimes disappear (pasting the feedback into chat works around it), very large repositories can cause lag, editing by several people at once is basic, the quality of an imported design system depends on the source files, and there is no version history yet.
Because there is no version history, export a PDF or HTML copy of any version you like before asking for big changes.

Claude Design is best treated as a fast sketching partner. Use it for a first draft, a pitch deck you need by tomorrow or a clickable prototype to test an idea. For production code, hand the design to Claude Code or a developer, and for a brand that has to look exactly right, keep a designer in the loop.
